title: Dots and vowels
hookLine: dots and vowel marks were added later to help new readers

cards: Three Arabic letters: ba, ta, tha. In a modern mushaf they have exactly the same shape, a little boat. The only difference is the dots: one below for ba, two above for ta, three above for tha.
Now take the dots away. That's close to what the earliest copies looked like: the bones of the words, with the reader supplying the rest from what they'd learned by ear.

teach.b: Early Arabic writing was a kind of shorthand. Many letters shared a shape, the dots that tell them apart were used sparingly, and short vowels weren't written at all.

teach.h: A PAGE THAT REMINDED, NOT TAUGHT
teach.b: For the first Muslims that wasn't a problem: the Qur'an lived in their mouths, learned from teachers, and the page was a reminder of what they already knew.
But as Islam spread to people whose first language wasn't Arabic, the tradition says, mistakes in recitation began.

Tradition credits a scholar of Basra, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, in the first Islamic century, with the first vowel marks: colored dots, often red, placed above, below or beside a letter to show its sound.
Later, in the time of the governor al-Hajjaj, scholars are said to have added the dots that tell similar letters apart more fully.

In the next century, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad of Basra, who also mapped the meters of Arabic poetry, gave the vowels the small shapes still used today: a slanting stroke above, a tiny curl like a waw, a stroke below.

But in every telling, the text itself stays put: the marks were added around it, like pronunciation guides on a poem for a new reader. Some scholars at the time disliked writing anything extra inside the mushaf.
In the end the community accepted the marks, because they served the recitation that had been passed down. Each dot was put there for a learner.

how: Muslims today read from copies with full dots and vowel marks, and learners, especially those who didn't grow up with Arabic, rely on those marks to recite correctly.

games.q: you teach the Qur'an in Basra. new Muslims who didn't grow up with Arabic keep misreading the vowels. what do you do?
o: change the words to easier ones.
add small marks to show the sounds.
games.why: tradition says that's exactly what Abu al-Aswad did: colored dots for the vowels, with the words untouched.

practice: If you have a mushaf or an app, open any page and just look, without trying to read: find the dots, one, two, three, above and below, and the tiny vowel strokes.
If there's no page in front of you, bring to mind ba, ta and tha, three little boats told apart only by their dots.

wordCard.voice: Tashkil. Vowel marking — the small strokes added to the Qur'an's script so new readers could recite it rightly. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: vowel marking, the small strokes that show short vowels. the dots that tell letters apart are called i'jam.
